name: temporal-property
intent: Give the few attributes of an object that change over time a normal-looking property interface whose accessors accept a time point, so callers can ask what the value was on a given date without knowing about, or searching, effective-dated records.
problem: A handful of attributes change over time and some consumers must read them as of past or future dates, but the model stores only current values - or exposes effectivity rows and history records to every caller - so each read re-implements an interval search and each new consumer gets the boundary rules slightly wrong.
context: Domain objects with a small number of temporal attributes (prices, salaries, addresses, rates, classifications) that must be reconstructable at a date, typically persisted in a relational store where the history becomes a history/intersection table; it also applies to in-memory models that accept scheduled future changes, and to master data that has to be reported as of a transaction date.
benefits: Callers ask domain questions in domain terms ('what did Mr Fowler's address look like on 2 Feb 1998?') with no knowledge of effectivity rows, revision numbers or interval boundaries.
The ordinary read path survives: the no-argument accessor defaults to today, so current-value code is unchanged.
History mechanics live in one place - the collection owns ordering, boundary search and range rewriting - instead of being repeated in every consumer.
Only the attributes that need history pay for it; the rest of the class stays a plain object.
A plain field refactors into a temporal one without changing the existing interface, so the pattern can be introduced late, when the need is proven.
The same interface supports retroactive corrections and future-dated (scheduled) changes, and upgrades to a bi-temporal or snapshot form when the first consumer needs wider reads.
tradeoffs: Every consumer now has two read forms to choose between, and the implicit default time point makes behaviour clock-dependent unless the time point is injected.

Insertion updates (correcting an existing range) are genuinely subtle: the value alone is not enough, because the same value can be valid in two disjoint ranges and the surrounding intervals must be adjusted.
The collection does not map naively to relational tables: you need an intersection/history table with explicit valid-from/valid-to columns, and some mapping code stays hand-written.

History grows with every change; as-of reads over audit/history tables are markedly slower than live reads (correlated subselects, unions of current and history), so indexing, partitioning and retention become design work.
Without a second time dimension, a retroactive correction silently overwrites what the system believed before, so older reports cannot be reproduced from the same store.
It is easy to apply to the wrong class: once most attributes are temporal the accessor pairs become clumsy and a versioned whole object (Temporal Object) is the better shape.
Historical values keep personal data alive after the current record is cleaned up, and an append-only store accumulates retention, privacy and tamper-resistance obligations.

participants.responsibility: The domain object that exposes the attribute: a date-parameterised accessor, a default-time accessor, and the put/update methods - and nothing about the history representation.
The ordered history store keyed by effective start date: get(time point), put(value, time point), a milestones traversal, and the range rewriting required by insertion updates.
The value type that indexes the property, with an explicit granularity (calendar date or instant) and an explicit bound convention - normally closed at the start, open at the end.
The immutable value valid during a period; it is never edited in place, because that would rewrite history without recording a version.

The persistence representation used when the collection is stored: a history/audit table, an intersection table with from/to columns, or the platform's system-versioned temporal table with an as-of query.

use_cases: Customer contact or address details where only the billing/shipping address needs historical reads.
Pay rates and salary history, including retroactive corrections after a promotion is back-dated.
Product price at the moment an order was placed, so an invoice can be reproduced from the catalogue's own history.
Reference data such as tax rates, tariffs or exchange rates that must be applied as of the transaction date.
Regulatory and audit reporting: reconstruct the state of a master record as of a quarter end, or as of the date a decision was taken.
Scheduled changes published in advance (a rate change effective next month) that must become current by the passage of time, with no update job.
Master-data reconciliation: which department, owner or classification a record held on a given date.

SQL Server / Azure SQL system-versioned temporal tables: PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME columns plus FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF reconstruct a row - and with it each of its attributes - as of a given instant, the platform realization the pattern's Effectivity/History Store participant hides behind the accessor pair.

django-simple-history: Model.history.as_of(t) (and instance .history.as_of(t)) returns the saved model as it existed at t, raising DoesNotExist if it did not exist then - a framework-level as-of accessor over an auto-maintained history table.

PostgreSQL 18+ application-time temporal tables: an attribute history stored as valid_at range rows guarded by PRIMARY KEY (id, valid_at WITHOUT OVERLAPS); ranges are half-open - inclusive start, exclusive end - so adjacent versions cover every date without overlapping (system time itself remains trigger/extension territory in PostgreSQL).
avoid_when: Nobody has asked for history yet: an audit log (or the ORM's revision table) plus a separate analysis path is cheaper than changing the model's read surface.
Most or all attributes of the object change over time, or the business speaks of versions (amendments, editions): use Temporal Object and version the whole object.
The domain genuinely needs explicit validity periods as first-class objects (employment periods, contract terms, assignments): plain Effectivity with a Range is simpler and more honest.
Only 'who changed what, when' is required and no past value ever has to answer a business question: framework auditing without an as-of accessor is enough.
The value changes continuously or is derived from an event stream (temperature, position, balance): use time-series storage or event sourcing, not a dated property.
anti_patterns: Recording every change in an audit log and calling the job done: the pattern's whole point is that the property itself answers the as-of question, and log processing is exactly the work it removes.
Making every attribute temporal because one attribute needed history - the object becomes a version store written as accessor pairs; that is Temporal Object territory.
Exposing the milestone list or the effectivity rows to callers 'for flexibility', so every consumer re-implements the boundary search with slightly different inclusive/exclusive rules.
Treating history rows as ordinary rows: updating or deleting them in place, so the store can no longer answer what was believed on a date.
Unbounded, unpartitioned, unpruned history tables advertised as compliance, with no retention or access strategy.
An implicit today inside domain logic (billing, settlement) instead of an injected time point, which makes results unreproducible after the fact.
design_principles: Information hiding: the temporal representation is private to the owner; callers see only the accessor pair.
Single responsibility: one collection owns ordering, boundary search and range rewriting.
Once and only once: the interval search is written once, not in every consumer of the property.
Interface stability: a plain attribute can be refactored into a temporal one without changing call sites.
Separation of concerns: temporal mechanics stay in the accessor; the domain decides policy (when a retroactive change is allowed, what is reported as of when).
Explicit time: the time point is a parameter of the read, not a hidden global.
best_practices: Always provide both accessors - parameterised by a time point and defaulting to today - and inject the time point in tests and replays instead of reading the clock inside domain logic.
Choose one granularity and one bound convention (date, [from, to) in half-open form) and state it once in the collection.
Key the store by effective start date and derive the end from the next milestone when at most one value can be valid at a time; keep explicit ranges when gaps or overlaps are meaningful.
Keep stored versions immutable and the store append-only; mutate by adding a version, never by editing a value.
Test the awkward cases explicitly: a date before the first version, a retroactive change that splits an interval, a future-dated change, and a value that is valid in two disjoint ranges.
Give history an owner and a policy: retention/pruning, partitioning and access control for historical values, so the store stays both useful and lawful.
When corrections must themselves be auditable, keep a second dimension (valid time plus recorded time) rather than overwriting the previous belief.
When persisted relationally, let the collection hide an intersection/history table (or the platform's system-versioned table plus its as-of query) - do not leak it into call sites.
sources: Fowler, M. - Temporal Property, eaaDev draft (2004): a property that changes over time; the accessor pair, additive vs insertion updates, the temporal collection and the bi-temporal extension.
Carlson, A., Estepp, S. & Fowler, M. - Temporal Patterns, PLoP'98 final submission P09: the original Temporal Property write-up (PropertyAllocation/DedicatedProperty, Snapshot).
Fowler, M. - Temporal Patterns narrative (eaaDev): how Temporal Property relates to Effectivity, Temporal Object and Snapshot.
Fowler, M. - Effectivity (eaaDev): validity ranges as the persistence-side representation the temporal collection hides.
Kulkarni, K. & Michels, J.-E. - Temporal features in SQL:2011, SIGMOD Record 41(3), 2012: system-versioned tables and the FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF query that database-backed realizations map onto.

Microsoft Learn - Querying data in a system-versioned temporal table: FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF reconstructs a row as of an instant; the vendor realization of the history table a stored temporal property maps onto.
django-simple-history - Querying History: history.as_of(t) returns an object as it existed at a time point (DoesNotExist if it did not exist then); a framework-level as-of accessor.

PostgreSQL documentation - Temporal Tables (application time) with the Release 18 notes: valid_at range columns, WITHOUT OVERLAPS temporal primary keys and foreign keys, half-open range convention; system time is documented as not yet core in PostgreSQL.

Kornelis, H. - Plansplaining part 18: Temporal tables (part 3), SQLServerFast.com: critique of as-of semantics - transaction-start timestamping, zero-duration intermediate versions hidden only by FOR SYSTEM_TIME filters, and the FROM..TO vs BETWEEN..AND boundary divergence.
